claim_paraphrase: The TRI page describes Munda clans as Killi, patrilineal in transmission, and traditionally associated with common ancestry and totemic origin.
The TRI page lists Mage Parab, Phagu, Karam, Baha Parab, Sarhul and Sohrai among festivals celebrated by Munda communities.
The TRI page reports durang for song and susun for dance, and lists Jadur, Karam Susun and Mage Susun as Munda dances.
The TRI page reports Cham utarna as a ceremony performed by the Pahan for the welfare and longevity of twins, described specifically for a brother-sister twin pair.
The TRI page identifies Lota-pani as an engagement ceremony.
The TRI page reports Dali Takka as a monetary gift generally paid to paternal guardians before marriage.
The TRI page describes marriage as a major life ritual and a week-long festivity.
The TRI page reports that scented oil and turmeric are applied to the face and body after death.
The TRI page states that widow marriage is common.
The TRI page describes Patthalgari as a stone-erection tradition associated with graves or village entrances, including genealogical inscriptions.
The TRI page identifies Horadiri as a stone on which a family tree is written.
The TRI page lists Chalpadiri or Saasandiri as a stone associated with marking village boundaries and limits.
The TRI page describes Ziddiri as a stone placed over the burial of the placenta and dried navel part of a newborn.
The Khunti district cultural profile describes Mundas as settled agriculturists, with forest-product collection and hunting, fishing and animal husbandry as supplementary activities.
The Khunti district profile states that the Pahan is the village priest at the Sarna sacred grove and worships village deities.
The Khunti district profile identifies Singbonga as the supreme benevolent deity in its description of Munda beliefs.
The Khunti district profile describes ancestral spirits (Ora Bongako) and states that their blessings are invoked in social and religious ceremonies.
The Khunti district profile describes Sarhul as a March–April flower festival in which Sal flowers are brought to the Sarna and the Pahan propitiates deities.
The Khunti district profile describes Mage as celebrated on the full moon day of Paush and associates it with spirits of deceased ancestors.
The Khunti district profile describes Karam in August–September, with a Karam sapling brought from the forest and overnight song/dance with rice beer.
The Khunti district profile describes Sohrai in October–November, including lighting lamps and washing cattle sheds.
Shekhar reports that both burial and cremation occur among Munda communities, with geographic and circumstantial variation.
Shekhar describes Umbul ader as a ceremony calling the spirit/shadow back to the house after burial in a documented Ranchi case.
Shekhar documents Hayom as a shaving-associated ceremony following Umbul ader, involving the Pahan and a symbolic clay effigy.
Shekhar documents Pathalgarri as erection of a megalithic monument for the dead in a Khunti case study.
Shekhar describes Jangtopa as a secondary/ceremonial bone-burial festival, with symbolic substitution possible when bones cannot be recovered.
Shekhar states that mortal remains of the same family may be buried under the same capstone or dolmen known as Saasandiri.
Shekhar reports that funerary treatment differs for deaths categorized as unnatural, including separate disposal locations and reduced ceremonial elaboration.
Shekhar reports variation in mortuary rites and monuments by age, status, economic condition, rank and circumstances of death.

A 2022 botany abstract reports that Munda rituals and festivals in Khunti are closely related to plants and explicitly mentions birth/naming, kanbhedi, marriage, godna, death and several festivals as contexts for ethnobotanical documentation.

A Jharkhand government page describes Sarhul with Sal flowers, Pahan fasting and worship, offerings, music, distribution of Sal flowers and Handia. The page explicitly addresses multiple tribal communities, so this record is contextual and requires Munda-specific field verification.
The Jharkhand government describes Karam as a youth-centered festival involving forest collection, worship, song and dance. This is contextual state-level evidence, not Munda-exclusive.
The Jharkhand government describes Sohrai as a cattle-care festival with lamps, washing cattle, vermilion-oil application and garlanding. This is contextual state-level evidence, not Munda-exclusive.

The 2025 publisher abstract reports continued construction of megalithic monuments among Munda communities in Jharkhand and frames them in the study as burial sites and markers of collective heritage. This is an abstract-level source report, not a universal or current-practice assertion beyond the study scope.
notes: Exact locator: publisher abstract at DOI 10.30884/seh/2025.02.01; full-text passage verification pending.

claim_label: Livelihood and non-wood forest products — 2021 article
claim_paraphrase: The publisher abstract reports that this Jharkhand-focused Munda study examines livelihood and sustainable-development perceptions, including forest preservation, women's role in livelihood development, and commercial or industrial use of non-wood forest products. This is an article-reported study characterization, not a universal or current community fact.
notes: Exact locator: Problems of Sustainable Development 16(1), 2021, pp. 181-185; abstract on p. 181; DOI 10.35784/pe.2021.1.19. Full methodological and participant-level extraction remains pending.

claim_label: Land and Munda-State relations — dissertation abstract
claim_paraphrase: The Virginia Tech dissertation abstract reports a fifteen-month ethnographic study conducted from May 2017 to December 2018 examining meanings of land for Munda participants in Jharkhand and how the author relates those meanings to Adivasi-State conflict, identity and representation. This is an author-reported study characterization, not a universal or current claim about all Munda communities.
notes: Exact locator: Virginia Tech VTechWorks institutional abstract, Handle 10919/111386. Participant-level propositions, quotations and local meanings require exact dissertation-page, ethics, consent, rights and cultural-access review.

claim_label: Mundari Khuntkatti study scope — publisher abstract
claim_paraphrase: The SAGE publisher abstract reports that the article examines Mundari Khuntkatti as a customary land institution and bases its empirical investigation on two Mundari Khuntkatti villages, Gutuhatu and Salga, in Khunti district. This record preserves the article author's framing and study scope; it is not a legal determination or a universal/current claim about all Munda communities.
geographic_scope: Gutuhatu and Salga, Khunti district, Jharkhand
notes: Exact locator: SAGE publisher abstract, The Oriental Anthropologist 13(2), pp. 267-280; DOI 10.1177/0972558X1301300205. Full-text passages, historical interpretation, participant data and current legal/community status remain unverified in MLHKP.

claim_paraphrase: The 2025 BMC Nutrition study reports a cross-sectional investigation of 201 Munda households in eleven villages in Murhu and Torpa blocks of Khunti district, with household surveys and seasonal food-frequency questionnaires used to derive dietary-pattern categories. This is a study-scope and method record, not a universal statement about Munda diets or current practice outside the sampled setting.
geographic_scope: Eleven villages, Murhu and Torpa blocks, Khunti district, Jharkhand
notes: Exact locators: PubMed abstract PMID 41121309 and PMC full-text Results opening (study conducted on 201 households of eleven villages in Murhu and Torpa); DOI 10.1186/s40795-025-01159-2. Participant-level data, culturally sensitive knowledge, community validation and extrapolation beyond the study are not inferred.

claim_label: Traditional food-environment study scope — 2021 Frontiers article
claim_paraphrase: The Frontiers article reports a cross-sectional mixed-methods study conducted in nine villages of Murhu and Torpa blocks in Khunti district, with data collection between June 2019 and January 2020 and multiple visits intended to capture seasonal food diversity. This record is limited to the article's documented study design and setting; it is not a universal claim about Munda food practices.
geographic_scope: Nine villages, Murhu and Torpa blocks, Khunti district, Jharkhand
notes: Exact locators: Frontiers full text, Abstract and Study Design sections; DOI 10.3389/fnut.2020.600470. Participant quotations, detailed indigenous-food lists, nutritional/medicinal implications, community validation and participant-level reuse permissions are not inferred.

claim_label: Comparative Adivasi women’s movements thesis scope
claim_paraphrase: The Sapienza institutional abstract reports that this dissertation examines Adivasi women’s movements from the 1980s onward in south Bihar and Jharkhand and explicitly includes Munda communities alongside Oraon, Santal and Ho communities. This is a source-scope record only; it does not transfer comparative findings to Munda women as a whole.
notes: Exact locator: Sapienza institutional abstract, Handles 20.500.14242/212639 and 11573/1740709. Munda-specific findings, named participants, interviews, images and field-derived propositions require exact chapter/page, ethics, consent, rights and cultural-access review before deeper ingestion.

claim_paraphrase: The ACL Anthology abstract reports an end-to-end text-to-speech system for Mundari, including collection and processing of Mundari text and speech data and evaluation using native-speaker judgments alongside objective metrics. This is a technical study-scope record, not a claim of community endorsement, dataset reuse permission, speaker representativeness, or a general linguistic or cultural property.
notes: Exact locator: ACL Anthology record 2024.computel-1.11, Abstract; proceedings pp. 76–82; DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.computel-1.11. Article-level CC BY does not establish rights over underlying recordings, datasets, model checkpoints or participant material; cultural access remains separately gated.

claim_label: Finger-millet value-chain study scope — 2022 Foods article
claim_paraphrase: The 2022 Foods article reports an exploratory value-chain case study of finger millet within a Munda community in Jharkhand. Its Methods section records in-person semi-structured interviews conducted January–April 2022 with 12 participants across village-leader, health/nutrition-worker and village-member stakeholder groups, with farming experience used for purposive selection. This record preserves the study design and sampled research context only; it is not a universal claim about Munda food practices or community endorsement.
notes: Exact locators: PMC9736962 Methods sections 2.1 and 2.4; DOI 10.3390/foods11233774. The article also documents ethics and consent procedures. Participant statements, transcripts, recordings, local-language content, cultural knowledge, underlying participant data and community validation are not promoted by this record.
